data.title: PMO adviser flags discom hurdles in expanding India's EV charging network
data.description:
Tarun Kapoor, advisor to the Prime Minister, on Friday flagged lack of cooperation from electricity distribution companies in scaling the electric vehicle charging network in the country.

He also said the government is open to additional funding for the charging infrastructure if required.

"DISCOMs sometimes are not very cooperative," Kapoor said while speaking at the SIAM's first Growth and Readiness for EV Infrastructure Dialogue on Friday.

According to him, distribution companies sometimes demand a substantial amount when setting up charging stations, particularly high capacity ones, and there is a need for a dedicated officer in every distribution company to address this issue.

"The cost of putting up a charging station as you all know the higher part of the cost is behind the metre where sometimes the distribution companies demand a huge amount of money," he said.

 

"Particularly if the charging station needs a higher capacity, say going to 100 KW or more then sometimes they ask for quite a huge amount of money." Kapoor noted that electric vehicles will be an important future source of electricity demand, creating a significant business opportunity for power distribution companies.

"We have been telling DISCOMs that now time has come to realise that EV is going to become one of their largest sectors for power consumption. And as a country we are entering a phase where there is surplus power available," he said.

Kapoor said the government is looking to encourage daytime charging rather than relying completely on overnight charging at homes. Charging facilities should increasingly be located at offices, workplaces, marketplaces and parking areas.

However, low utilisation at some of the existing public charging stations is also a concern, which impacts their maintenance and long-term viability.

Kapoor said some charging stations had utilisation levels of less than 1 per cent, making maintenance difficult for operators.

Adoption of electric vehicles in India is at an early stage, with faster adoption seen in two and three-wheeler segments. Charging infrastructure is one of the key bottlenecks to wider adoption.

Under the Rs 11,900 crore PM E-Drive scheme, the government has set aside Rs 2,000 crore to subsidise charging infrastructure, including up to 72,300 new public EV charging stations, battery swapping stations, and battery charging stations.

"There is a good amount of money available going forward to establish charging infrastructure. And I think the government would be willing to put in more funds also if need be," he added.

data.title: Sensex zooms 1790 pts in 2 days; ₹6.9 trn added to m-cap: 5 key reasons
data.description:
The Indian benchmark indices are on a winning streak as they gained nearly 1 per cent in Friday's intraday session, extending rise to the second day. Meanwhile, they have risen in four of the five trading sessions this week.
 
In intraday deals, 30-pack Sensex added 803 points or 0.97 per cent to hit the day's high of 83,825. In last trade, it gained 990 points, taking the two-day rise to 1,793 points or 2.2 per cent.
 
Similarly, its NSE counterpart Nifty 50 gained 231 points or 0.90 per cent during the day to rise to the day's peak of 25,746. In a span of two days it has gained 518 points or 2.05 per cent.
 
 
During this period, the market capitalisation of BSE-listed stocks has increased by ₹6.90 trillion from ₹506.47 trillion on Wednesday to ₹513.37 trillion today.  
 
Both the benchmark indices are now less than 3 per cent from reclaiming their all-time high levels. The sharp nearly 12 per cent rise seen in November has helped them rebound after a prolonged phase of consolidation.
 

What's driving Indian stock markets?

Here are key factors behind the rise in the Sensex and Nifty today:
 
1. Bank stocks rally
Index-heavyweight banks and financials emerged as the top contributors to the rise seen in the flagship indices today. HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Kotak Bank and Axis Bank alone contributed over 500 points or nearly 65 per cent gains seen in the Sensex today.  
 
The sharp rally in leading private bank stocks has also driven the Nifty Bank above the 64,000 mark for the first time. Data for the first fortnight of November shows that financial services attracted the bulk of the FII inflows at ₹43,102 crore.
 
FIIs are now buying the very same stocks they have been selling to raise money for the AI trade, said Dr VK Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist, Geojit Investment.
 
2. FPI buying
November has seen record buying from foreign investors, with NSDL showing net inflows of 1.14 trillion - the highest ever in a month till date. Strong FPI interest has been a major driver for the Indian equity market, especially as they pivot away from AI-related bets in global markets.
 
"FII buying is so sustained and aggressive that the bulls are calling the shots. Despite occasional dips, the market is likely to remain resilient on the back of massive FII flows assisted by impressive corporate earnings," said Vijayakumar.
 
3. Oil weakness
The oil prices are set for a weekly decline even as they eked out minor gains today. Lower crude oil prices bode well for import-focussed economies like India as it improves the macroeconomic outlook and strengthens the current account deficit.
 
Currently, oil prices are hovering around $92 a barrel, and analysts expect the prices to head lower in the coming year amid supply glut. The IEA's November report puts October supply at 105.4 mb/d and shows observed inventories rising 52 million barrels, the first build since June.
 
Mirae Asset Sharekhan said it expects Brent to end 2027 near $78.
 
4. Earnings growth strong
Elara Capital said that India’s resilient earnings trajectory has been instrumental in anchoring the downside for Indian equities. With earnings revisions gaining positive momentum, even a modest easing of external headwinds could set the stage for a market re-rating, it noted in a note recently.
 
Despite a weaker rupee, a Brent spike above $100/bbl, higher global yields and supply disruptions from the West Asia conflict, the Elara Universe posted robust sales/EBITDA/PAT growth of 23.8%/25.7%/28.7% YoY in Q2FY27.
 
5. Technical outlook
Commenting on the technical outlook, SBI Securities said that for Nifty 50, the zone of 25400-25420 will act as a crucial support for the index, while the resistance lies in the zone of 25,710-25,730.
 
In the event of a surge above 25,730, the index can experience an extension of the rally towards 25,800, it opined. On the downside, if the index slips below the level of 25,400, then the next support is placed in the zone of 25,230-25,250.
 
Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion.

data.title: Cauvery dispute: SC dismisses Tamil Nadu's pleas for 11 TMC water release
data.description:
The Supreme Court on Friday dismissed two pleas of the Tamil Nadu government seeking a direction to Karnataka for the release of 11 thousand million cubic (TMC) feet of Cauvery river water.

A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Aparesh Kumar Singh said that Tamil Nadu has filed a third application for bringing on record some additional documents, which will also be dismissed.

In its pleas, the Tamil Nadu government sought directions to Karnataka to make sure that the backlog of 11 TMC of Cauvery water as on October 7 is cleared immediately and ensure the same at the rate of 1.3 TMC per day in 10 days at Billigundulu, a key water-measuring station on the banks of the river along the Karnataka-Tamil Nadu border.

 

On October 12, the top court reserved its decision on the two applications of the Tamil Nadu government.

The Karnataka government had told the top court that it would be difficult to meet Tamil Nadu's demand for the release of 11 TMC feet of Cauvery river water for making good a "shortfall" as this was a rain-deficit year and several areas have been declared drought-affected.

The Tamil Nadu government said it is only seeking its legitimate pro-rata share in the flows realised during the distress period, together with the backlog due to it, and the entire burden of meteorological and hydrological distress cannot be passed on to the lower riparian state, while Karnataka continues to utilise the available storage and inflows for irrigation and other requirements.

During the hearing, counsel for the Karnataka government submitted that this has been a very difficult year and several areas have been declared drought-hit.

"We have to ensure conservation of water so that the drinking water supply in residential areas is not affected," he had said, adding that Tamil Nadu has the benefit of the northeast monsoon in November, when its reservoirs will be replenished, while it will not help Karnataka.

"Every distress year, this has been the problem," he had said, adding that there has been proper application of mind by the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) at its 59th meeting held on October 8, in which it directed Karnataka to release 3,000 cusecs of Cauvery water at Billigundulu from October 9 for the next 15 days.

The counsel for the Tamil Nadu government had contended that Karnataka be directed to release the shortfall on a pro-rata basis, else crops in the state would be affected this year.

He said they cannot wait for another year as farmers in Tamil Nadu are facing a tough time and urged the court to at least make some interim arrangements.

In its plea filed through standing counsel B Karunakaran, the Tamil Nadu government said that, at a meeting held on September 24, the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee (CWRC), based on the percentage of deficit, found that the flow realised at Billigundulu should have been 52.935 TMC and that there is a shortfall in the realisation of flows.

"In spite of noting the said deficit, the CWRC did not take any decision with regard to directing Karnataka to make good the shortfall and proceeded to reduce the flows from 6,000 cusecs to 4,000 cusecs. The CWRC directed Karnataka to ensure releases from its reservoirs so that 4,000 cusecs are received at Billigundulu in the next 15 days (effective September 24)," it said.

Giving the data of water release, the Tamil Nadu government said that even then, Karnataka did not adhere to the CWRC's directions and failed to ensure 4,000 cusecs every day.

It pointed out that Tamil Nadu's share in this distress year has to be decided on a pro-rata basis, but the CWMA, even after eight years since its constitution, has failed to formulate the distress formula -- a formula to share water during distress years, without any ambiguity or unfair treatment to a particular state.

It said the water directed to be released by the CWMA -- 4,000 cusecs at Billigundulu for 15 days starting September 24 and 3,000 cusecs from October 9 -- is grossly inadequate and does not redress the substantial backlog already accumulated.

The Tamil Nadu government said on October 8, the CWRC did not take any decision with regard to directing Karnataka to make good the shortfall and proceeded to reduce the flows from 4,000 cusecs to 3,000 cusecs effective October 9.

It sought directions to the Karnataka government to ensure and implement the CWMA's decision dated September 24 and make good the shortfall of 0.94 TMC towards the non-supply of water for the period from September 24 to October 7, and further flows as directed by the CWMA in its minutes dated October 8.

On September 24, the court asked the Karnataka government to respond to Tamil Nadu's plea seeking the release of its share of Cauvery water, alleging a shortfall in supply.

While the Tamil Nadu government told the court that it has already lost an early Kharif crop due to the lack of water, Karnataka said it is facing a "terrible drought situation".

The Tamil Nadu government approached the apex court on August 3, seeking directions to Karnataka for the immediate release of the water.

In its plea, Tamil Nadu has claimed that the quantum allocated to it by the CWRC as well as that released by its neighbour, Karnataka, is very little.

data.title: SatSure targets ₹200 cr in Series B to expand satellite and AI capabilities
data.description:
The Antariksh Venture Capital Fund (AVCF), backed by the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) and managed by SIDBI Venture Capital Ltd (SVCL), is investing ₹60 crore in Bengaluru-based Earth-intelligence startup SatSure, leading the first close of its ₹200 crore Series B funding round.
 
The transaction marks AVCF's first investment in the downstream data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI) layer of India's space economy, extending its investment footprint beyond launch and satellite hardware into commercial space-data infrastructure serving enterprise and sovereign markets.
 
“The Antariksh Venture Capital Fund is mandated to catalyse India’s private space ecosystem from proven technical capability to global commercial scale,” said Arup Kumar, managing director and chief executive officer of SIDBI Venture Capital Ltd.
 
 
“Leading SatSure’s Series B round reflects AVCF’s thesis of backing full-stack enterprises that pair indigenous orbital infrastructure with downstream decision intelligence. As India’s space economy matures, AVCF will continue deploying patient institutional growth capital behind space-tech companies built to compete internationally,” he said.
 
AVCF's investment will support four priorities for SatSure, in line with India's space commercialisation roadmap.
 
These include advancing its optical payloads ahead of a planned orbital flight in 2027 and executing a multi-satellite constellation mandate under the IN-SPACe-anchored Earth Observation Public-Private Partnership (EO-PPP).
 
The funding will also support the scaling of Dhaarini, SatSure's Large Earth Observation Model, which had earlier received a ₹24.6 crore grant under IN-SPACe's Technology Adoption Fund (TAF).
 
The company also plans to expand its international commercial operations from India.
 
SatSure's ongoing ₹200 crore Series B round comprises ₹165 crore in primary equity, ₹25 crore in venture debt and ₹10 crore in secondary transactions. The company expects to close the round on a rolling basis through December 2026.
 
Following the first close, SatSure's cumulative institutional capital raised stands at ₹427 crore, excluding government grants.
 
SatSure operates a full-stack Earth intelligence business through two entities.
 
Its subsidiary KaleidEO develops optical satellite payloads and builds complete satellites under India's Earth Observation Public-Private Partnership for the national Earth observation constellation.
 
SatSure, meanwhile, converts Earth observation data into decision intelligence for banks, insurers, critical infrastructure companies and governments.
 
Its operations span the value chain from satellite payloads and geospatial foundation models to AI, analytics and industry-specific applications.
 
“The strategic value of the space economy lies not only in reaching orbit, but in what we can understand from it. That intelligence is reliable only when you own the full chain behind it: from the payloads in orbit, to the AI and foundation models that turn that data into decisions enterprises and governments act on,” said Prateep Basu, chief executive officer and co-founder of SatSure.
 
“We built SatSure to own that full stack end-to-end, and the Series B round lets us build it further, from India, for the world,” he added.
 
SatSure's Earth intelligence technology is already integrated into India's financial infrastructure.
 
Its SatSource product line is part of the Reserve Bank of India's Unified Lending Interface (ULI).
 
Public-sector banks, including State Bank of India, use the platform to assess farm loan applications in minutes, a process that earlier took weeks, according to the company.
 
SatSure has 24 banking and financial services customers. These include HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank, both of which are investors in as well as customers of the company.
 
SatSure's earlier funding rounds were backed by Baring Private Equity Partners India, Promus Ventures, Asian Development Bank Ventures, Omidyar Network India, now Prana Ventures, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank and Nuvama Asset Management, among others.
 
India's space economy is projected to expand from around $8.4 billion in 2023 to $40-45 billion by 2030, according to a Jefferies report.
 
The government has set a target of building a $100 billion space economy by 2040.
 
The number of registered space startups in India has increased from one in 2014 to around 440 as of August 2026, according to government data.
 
Nine startups identified by Jefferies have collectively raised about $539 million, while cumulative private investment in the broader ecosystem reached nearly $600 million by FY26.
 
Among the leading companies, Skyroot Aerospace has raised $160 million, Pixxel $95 million, Agnikul Cosmos $76 million and Digantara $65 million.

data.title: IITF 2026: All you need to know about tickets, timings and entry gates
data.description:
The 45th edition of the India International Trade Fair (IITF) opened to the general public at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on November 19. The annual event, organised by the India Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO), will continue until November 27.
 
This fair has attracted significant attention from the capital city as well as the wider domestic and international business sectors. 
 
If you intend to attend the trade fair with your family or friends, remember to check ticket prices, visiting hours, entry points, and specific attractions within the halls. IITF is hosting exhibitors from India and abroad who are ready to welcome visitors as the fair gets underway. 
 

IITF 2026 dates and timings

The ongoing edition of the IITF is taking place from November 14 to November 27, covering a total of 14 days. This year, the event has been separated into two segments to cater to both business attendees and the general public. 
 
The initial 5 days, running from November 14 to 18, were specifically allocated for business attendees and trade exhibitors. 
 
From November 19, the fair has opened its doors to the general public, welcoming families and younger guests, and will continue to do so until November 27. The fair will operate daily from 10 am until 7:30 pm, allowing entry until 5:30 pm. 
 
Each year, the trade fair draws in numerous visitors. Measures have been implemented to handle the crowd and ensure a smooth experience for all attendees.

How to book IITF 2026 tickets and ticket prices?

Visitors can buy tickets through an online platform from home. Those who prefer to acquire tickets in person can go to ticket counters established at 55 metro stations throughout the Delhi-NCR region. 
 
Visitors should be aware that the Supreme Court metro station, which is nearest to Bharat Mandapam, will not have a ticket counter for IITF. 
 
To enhance the experience for attendees, the India Trade Promotion Organisation (ITPO) has launched the IITF 2026 mobile app. This app allows visitors to find details regarding exhibitors, exhibition halls, event venues, and available products.

IITF 2026 Ticket Prices

The ticket prices for the general public are from November 19 to 27 are as below:
 
Adults: Rs 100 on weekdays and Rs 200 on Saturdays and Sundays.
 
Children: Rs 50 on weekdays and Rs 100 on Saturdays and Sundays.
 
Senior citizens and persons with disabilities: Free entry with a valid government identity card.
 
Fair timings: 10 am to 7:30 pm 
Last entry: 5:30 pm. 

IITF 2026: Entry Gates And Security Arrangements

To maintain safety and facilitate visitor movement, gates 3, 4, 6, and 10 have been identified as the primary access points for the trade fair. 
 
Attendees arriving in personal automobiles should know that their vehicles will be subjected to security inspections at specified parking locations before gaining access. 
 
Security personnel and the trade fair organizers have put in place plans to handle the anticipated number of visitors and guarantee efficient movement throughout the venue.

IITF 2026: Which state will be showcased in which hall?

Hall 1: This hall will present Jharkhand, Jammu and Kashmir and Meghalaya, along with exhibitions by international exhibitors and companies worldwide.
 
Hall 2: Visitors can explore states including Delhi, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Gujarat, Ladakh, Manipur, Punjab and Telangana.
 
Hall 3: This hall will display Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Nagaland, Odisha, Puducherry, Tripura and Uttar Pradesh, offering a glimpse of their culture and development.
 
Hall 4: Stalls and exhibits from Assam, Chhattisgarh, Chandigarh and Madhya Pradesh will be showcased here.
 
Hall 5: Visitors can explore products and cultural displays from West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh and Karnataka.
 
Hall 6: The hall will explore the Khadi Gramodyog.

data.title: India's wheat acreage may see steepest fall in 26 years on water shortage
data.description:
India's wheat acreage is poised for its steepest decline in 26 years as fields parched by the weakest monsoon rains in more than a decade spur farmers ​to switch to competing crops in search of better returns, industry officials told ​Reuters.

The drop in planting, coupled with the risk of lower yields brought by a severe El Niño ‌weather pattern, threatens to curb output in the world's second-largest wheat producer, in turn boosting prices and complicating efforts to damp food inflation.

"Wheat needs to be irrigated at least four to five times, but we don't have enough water even to sow the crop," said farmer Vilas Bhutekar in the Jalna district of the western state of Maharashtra.

 

"So we chose chickpeas instead, as they require less water."

India's main winter-sown crop, wheat usually competes for acreage with rapeseed, chickpeas and corn.

India's June-September monsoon rains were the lowest in more than a decade as the drying effect of the El Niño drove rainfall as much as 41 per cent below average in key wheat-growing states such as Punjab, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra.

"Wheat needs more water than other competing ‌crops," said Nitin Gupta, deputy country head at agricultural trader Olam Agri India.

"But water is in short supply in some regions this year, which could mean farmers plant less wheat."

Wheat was planted across 5 million hectares (12 million acres) by Nov. 13, down 15.3 per cent from a year earlier, government data show.

Planting for the 2026/27 season is expected to fall about 6 per cent from last year's record of 33.6 million hectares (83 million acres), an average estimate by 10 industry officials shows.

That would be the steepest decline since 2000/01, taking area under the crop to the lowest ​in four years at 31.58 million hectares (78 million acres).

Crop shift

Wheat acreage is expected to stay largely steady in the key ‌northern states of Haryana and Punjab, which have access to reliable irrigation.

But farmers in other states are likely to shift from wheat to less-thirsty crops such as chickpea and rapeseed, industry officials said.

Prices of these crops ​have risen much ‌more than wheat, prompting farmers to shift acreage away from the grain, said Sandeep Bansal, director of a flour miller ‌based in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh.

"Wheat is usually farmers' first choice, but this year other crops are giving better returns," Bansal said.

The state-run Food Corporation of India buys wheat from farmers at the minimum ‌support ​price, which New ​Delhi raised this year by just 1 per cent to 2,610 rupees per 100 kg, the smallest increase since 2002/03.

"The government typically incentivises wheat planting by raising procurement prices by 5 to 6 per cent annually," said ‌a New Delhi-based trader ​with a global trade house.

"This year's 1 per cent hike is, in fact, discouraging farmers from expanding wheat acreage."

data.title: India's energy demand to grow 3 times faster than global average: IEA
data.description:
The West Asia conflict has exposed vulnerabilities in global energy supply chains, with disruptions to key shipping routes raising concerns about the availability and cost of oil and gas. The International Energy Agency’s (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2026 examines how the duration of the crisis could shape global energy markets and influence countries' energy strategies.
 
The report also highlights India's growing energy needs, projecting that the country will account for more growth in energy demand over the next decade than any other country or region. Meeting this demand while ensuring reliable and affordable supplies will be a key challenge as India seeks to diversify its energy mix and reduce its exposure to external disruptions.
 
 

West Asia crisis shakes global energy markets

 
The scale of the disruption is reflected in the cumulative loss of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) of natural gas from the Gulf since the crisis began, according to the IEA. By November 2026, the disruption to energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz was still continuing, with the impact increasingly being passed on to consumers through higher prices as supply buffers ran down.
 
The pressure has been particularly severe in Asia, which accounted for around 80 per cent of the oil and nearly 90 per cent of the liquefied natural gas (LNG) that passed through the Strait before the crisis. Diesel supplies have also come under significant pressure, with prices crossing $200 per barrel.
 
The crisis is also prompting Gulf producers to reconsider their dependence on the Strait. According to the IEA, countries in the region are constructing or considering alternative pipeline projects with a combined capacity of around 7 million barrels per day. These projects could require investments of about $40 billion and add around $2 per barrel to export costs.
 
The IEA expects the disruption to have lasting implications for global energy trade, with countries increasingly looking to diversify suppliers, transport routes and energy sources. Solar power and nuclear energy could benefit from this shift, while faster electrification is emerging as another way to reduce exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets.
 
For India, these changes carry particular significance. As one of the world's largest energy consumers and importers, the country faces the dual challenge of securing supplies amid geopolitical uncertainty and meeting rapidly rising domestic demand.
 

India's energy demand to surge

 
India is expected to record more growth in energy demand over the next decade than any other country or region, according to the IEA. The country's energy consumption is projected to grow by 2.5 per cent annually until 2035 under the Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), around three times the global rate.
 
The increase will be driven by rising incomes, urbanisation, industrial expansion and growing demand for cooling and mobility. The IEA estimates that India will:
 
  • Add more than 12,000 cars to its roads every day over the next decade
  • See a 33 per cent increase in built-up spaces
  • Install an additional 200 million air conditioners in homes
  • Expand production of energy-intensive materials such as iron, steel and cement
 
This growth will put additional pressure on India's energy infrastructure and increase the need for reliable and affordable supplies.
 
However, India's dependence on imported fuels makes it particularly vulnerable to global disruptions. The country imports around 40 per cent of its overall energy requirements, including 90 per cent of its crude oil and 50 per cent of its natural gas.
 
The recent disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has highlighted this exposure, particularly for cooking gas. Around half of the LPG cylinders used by Indian households depend on supplies passing through the strategic waterway. LPG imports fell by more than 50 per cent during the first two months of the conflict, prompting the government to maximise domestic production and prioritise household supplies.
 

India's energy mix gets greener

 
Despite its growing energy requirements, India is making progress in diversifying its energy mix. Solar power accounted for half of the country's power capacity additions over the past decade, while India achieved its target of having 50 per cent of installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources in 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
 
The IEA expects electricity demand to grow by 6 per cent annually over the next decade as transport, buildings and industries increasingly shift towards electricity.
 
Under the STEPS, India's electricity generation is projected to increase from 2,114 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025 to 3,585 TWh by 2035. The share of non-fossil sources, including renewables and nuclear power, is expected to rise from around 28 per cent to 51 per cent over the same period.
 
However, coal will continue to play an important role in India's energy system because of its substantial domestic reserves. The IEA expects coal to increasingly provide flexibility to the power system as renewable energy capacity expands.
 

Dependence on imported fuels

 
India had nearly 6 million barrels per day (mb/d) of refining capacity in 2025, making it the world's fourth-largest country by refining capacity and third-largest by refinery runs. It is also the second-largest net crude oil importer after China.
 
With another 840,000 barrels per day of refining capacity under construction, India is expected to strengthen its role as an exporter of petroleum products, particularly diesel and other middle distillates.
 
However, the IEA projects that domestic crude oil production will decline by nearly 20 per cent by 2035 under the STEPS, while refining capacity expands by one million barrels per day. This will increase the country's overall crude import requirements, even as imports from West Asia remain broadly stable.
 
Cooking gas presents another challenge. India is the world's second-largest LPG importer, with domestic production meeting around 40 per cent of demand in 2025.
 
Under the STEPS, LPG demand is expected to grow by almost 400,000 barrels per day by 2035, while domestic supply increases by less than 100,000 barrels per day. Consequently, LPG imports could rise to nearly 1 million barrels per day.
 
The IEA also highlights a potential trade-off for refiners, as increasing LPG production could come at the expense of higher-value products such as diesel and petrol.
 

A faster shift to clean energy

 
The IEA's Additional Response Case (ARC) examines how faster adoption of clean energy, efficiency measures and domestic resources could reduce India's exposure to imported fuels.
 
Under this scenario, electric cars are adopted 30 per cent faster by 2035 than under the STEPS, while electrification and energy efficiency in industry accelerate. India could reduce its oil requirements by 580,000 barrels per day and natural gas consumption by 8 per cent compared with the STEPS by 2035.
 
This would also help bring LPG imports below 750,000 barrels per day, compared with nearly 1 million barrels per day under the STEPS.
 
The report suggests that faster electrification, greater use of renewables and improved energy efficiency could bring India closer to its ambition of achieving energy independence by 2047. However, the transition will require substantial investment in electricity infrastructure, domestic energy production and supply-chain diversification.

data.title: UP CM Yogi Adityanath's mother Savitri Devi passes away in Uttarakhand
data.description:
Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath's mother, Savitri Devi, died on Friday in her native village in Pauri Garhwal district.

Pauri Garhwal SSP Sarvesh Panwar said she died in Panchur village of the district and the local administration was in touch with the family members. The last rites are likely to take place in Haridwar on Saturday.

In a social media post, Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said, "The news of the demise of Savitri Devi ji, the respected mother of Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh, Yogi Adityanath ji, is extremely sad and heartbreaking." Dhami said mother's love, blessings and affection are the most precious assets of life. "Her demise is an irreparable loss to the family." "I pray to Baba Kedar to give a place to the departed soul and provide strength to the bereaved family members, including Yogi ji to bear this immense loss," he added.

data.title: Asset allocation, rebalancing key to wealth creation over 3-5 yrs: Dezerv
data.description:
With a large number of wealth products available to investors, deciding where to invest, how much, and when to change course is now the harder problem, says Sandeep Jethwani, Co-founder, Dezerv, in an email interaction with Saloni Goel. He adds that personalisation will be the next big battleground for wealth management companies going forward. Edited excerpts: 
With rising life expectancy, healthcare costs, and inflation, how should investors approach retirement corpus planning? Is there any one figure or number that helps your clients plan better? 
Start with your own number, not the country’s. Most investors plan with national averages, or with a figure that felt comfortable a few years ago, and both understate what they will need. In 2006, ₹1 crore sounded like a safe retirement corpus. Twenty years on, the same lifestyle needs closer to ₹6 crore. 
 
Your number depends on four inputs: what you spend today, how fast that spending grows, when you stop earning, and how long you live after that. Household spending in India has compounded at over 9 per cent a year for five decades, and an affluent family’s costs, led by private healthcare at 12-14 per cent, rise faster still. On longevity, plan to 90, not to the national average.
Put those inputs together, and you arrive at your number.  
What are the biggest mistakes Indian investors make when estimating their retirement needs? 
The most common mistake is never estimating at all. Most investors have a sense that they are saving enough without having worked out what enough means for their household. 
The second is using the wrong inputs. People plan with 5-6 per cent inflation because that is the headline figure, while their own spending grows much faster. They also assume expenses will fall after retirement. In practice, travel and healthcare replace what EMIs and the office commute used to cost. And they plan to the average lifespan, when national averages say very little about how long a healthy urban professional is likely to live. 
ALSO READ: Stock Market LIVE: Sensex jumps 700 pts, Nifty above 25,700; IT, bank, realty shares outperform
 
The third is assuming the earning years will last as long as they did for the previous generation. AI adoption in India is among the highest globally, and careers in several sectors could compress by five to ten years. That means fewer years to save and more years to fund. 
Each of these mistakes makes the number look smaller than it is, and the gap usually shows up when it is too late to close. 
Investors today have access to a growing range of wealth products. What are the factors that determine whether an investor should opt for a customised wealth solution over a mutual fund portfolio? 
Good outcomes depend on three things: advice, decision, and execution.  
A mutual fund gives you professional management within the fund. It does not decide how much of your wealth belongs in that fund, when to rebalance your portfolio, or what to change when your life changes. Those calls still rest with you. 
Four factors usually tip the balance towards a customised solution. The first is the complexity of the wealth itself. Once a family holds equity, bonds, real estate, ESOPs, a business stake and loans across several platforms, nobody owns the aggregate view, and that is where most portfolios drift. The second is time and temperament. Many of our clients are money-rich and time-poor; they can make sound decisions but struggle to execute them consistently through a full market cycle. The third is tax, because a customised portfolio can coordinate gains, losses and rebalancing across the whole book rather than one product at a time. The fourth is life stage. A liquidity event, a transition into retirement, or a large liability changes the right allocation, and someone needs to be accountable for acting on it. 
One caution. A wider product shelf is not, by itself, a reason to own more products or to customise.  
What are the biggest structural changes you expect in India’s wealth management industry over the next five years?  
Three shifts stand out. 
The first is a move from selling individual products to managing outcomes. The next five years will be organised around who takes responsibility for a family’s portfolio as a whole. This matters most for India’s first-generation wealth creators: doctors, lawyers, senior professionals, founders and employees monetising ESOPs. The proposed new mutual fund-only PMS (PRIM) at ₹25 lakh brings this within reach of a much wider base of investors. I expect most serious wealth managers to offer portfolio management solutions of their own. 
The second is transparency as the default. The new wealth creator is also younger (the average Dezerv client is 38) and far more willing to ask what they pay and what they receive for it. Every model in the industry will need a clear answer.
 The third is digital by default. India has roughly one crore households with financial assets above ₹1 crore, and only around 10,000 relationship managers to serve them. Hiring alone cannot fix that arithmetic. Digital also changes how trust is built. Clients today would rather have a structured 30-minute call than a two-hour meeting, and once the digital experience is good, most HNIs no longer need to meet in person.  
What are the three biggest changes Indian investors should make to their portfolios over the next three to five years? 
First, move from collecting products to owning an allocation. More funds and products rarely add diversification. They usually add overlap. Consolidate, and let an asset allocation tied to your goals drive what you hold. 
Second, rebuild the middle of the portfolio. Many Indian investors hold equity on one side and fixed deposits on the other, with little in between. Debt funds, high-quality bonds, SIFs, InvITs, REITs and gold in measured proportions can improve both income and resilience.  
Third, stop investing through the rear-view mirror. Money tends to arrive after the move has happened. 
Over the next three to five years, asset allocation & disciplined rebalancing will matter more than any single call. 
How do you assess the growth of platform-based wealth management companies? Will the next battleground be product distribution, portfolio management, or personalised advice? 
Platforms like Groww and Zerodha have done the Indian investor a great service. They solved access. Anyone with a phone can now buy a stock or a mutual fund in minutes at very low cost, and that has brought crores of first-time investors into the market. 
Solving access exposed the next bottleneck, whichis choice. India has more mutual fund schemes than genuinely investable stocks, thousands of bonds, and a growing range of AIFs, REITs and InvITs. Deciding where to invest, how much, and when to change course is now the harder problem. 
I do not think distribution is the next battleground, because distribution is fast becoming a utility with tech. Advice on its own will not settle it either. The battleground is personalised portfolio management: advice, decision and execution held by one accountable party, with the portfolio built around an individual’s goals, liabilities and existing holdings. 
Technology makes this possible at scale for the first time. Personalisation used to be reserved for the very wealthy because it was expensive to deliver. Data and AI change that cost structure. The market is large enough for several models to succeed.

data.title: Brent seen at $75-85 in 2027 as oil surplus builds: Mirae Asset Sharekhan
data.description:
Disclaimer: Views and outlook in this report belong to the brokerages and analysts cited. They do not reflect the views of Business Standard. Readers are advised to exercise discretion. Oil has spent November unwinding the fear it priced in during October. Brent has fallen nearly 19 per cent, from around $118 a barrel in late October to $95, and both Brent and WTI have corrected 15 per cent in a month while still up 50 per cent for the year. In the physical market, Dated Brent, which traded $25-30 a barrel above futures at the end of October, now trades less than a dollar away. The Republican defeat in the US midterms eased fears of a wider US-Iran war, and much of the geopolitical premium went with it. On Thursday, reports that President Trump is weighing further strikes on Iran lifted prices only until the US, China and Russia agreed to boost production and supply of refined products. A market that shrugs off war headlines has stopped paying for scarcity.
 
 
Refining economics have deflated alongside crude. The benchmark 3-2-1 crack spread has corrected 22 per cent in a month, US gasoline has eased to $3.82 a gallon and diesel has slipped below $6. Yet gasoline is still 24 per cent more expensive than a year ago and diesel nearly 60 per cent higher. Global crude processing capacity was still down 2.5 per cent at the end of the third quarter, and Ukrainian drone attacks on 13 Russian refineries since November began have cut Russian runs to 4.2 million barrels a day (mb/d) from 5 mb/d in late October. Crude can be plentiful while diesel and jet fuel stay scarce.
 
Iran has stepped up attacks on Hormuz shipping and struck US facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait, while Saudi Arabia faces daily Houthi drone and missile attacks. The International Energy Agency (IEA) puts October Gulf oil exports excluding Oman at 18.4 mb/d, still about 26 per cent below pre-war, with crude flows back to 15 mb/d, roughly 82 per cent of pre-war volumes in October but have once again receded to 8-9mbpd. Saudi crude production rose 970,000 b/d to 9.2 mb/d, up from a 36-year low in August; Iraq is pumping at a seven-year high and Kirkuk–Ceyhan is flowing again. The mix is changing: in early November, Gulf crude exports excluding Iran ran about 2.0 mb/d below October, while refined-product exports climbed to about 65 per cent of pre-war levels. Gulf-to-China supertanker rates are down almost a quarter from October's record.
 The IEA's November report puts October supply at 105.4 mb/d and shows observed inventories rising 52 million barrels, the first build since June. It expects fourth-quarter supply of about 105 mb/d to exceed demand by roughly 1.7 mb/d, sees 2026 demand falling 2.7 mb/d to 102.3 mb/d, and projects a larger surplus in 2027. That assumes Gulf exports stay 26 per cent below pre-war; meanwhile. OPEC's October crude output rose 930,000 b/d to an eight-month high of 22.8 mb/d, and OPEC+ production of about 41.23 mb/d is near pre-war levels.
 
Asia shows both sides of the trade. China's refining system, the world's largest at roughly 18–19m b/d, is running below 80 per cent of capacity, with independents at just 56 per cent, and Chinese gasoline and diesel demand is forecast to fall about 9.5 per cent this year as EVs and LNG trucks spread. Beijing is exporting the surplus: it added 5.68m tonnes of export quota, and November export plans are up 25 per cent, with gasoline doubling. India is the mirror image. October consumption rose 2.7 per cent year on year to 20.494 million tonnes, the highest for the month, led by a 12.0 per cent jump in diesel. Yet India's crude basket has climbed from an average of $89 to $96, and elevated shipping and insurance costs weigh on the rupee, the deficits and inflation. China is exporting spare capacity.
 
US weekly data point the same way. As of 13 November, crude inventories were 3.6 per cent below the five-year seasonal average and gasoline 2.3 per cent above, but distillates were 7.0 per cent below. Crude production rose 0.1 per cent to a record high, and refinery utilisation was 92.8 per cent in the week to 23 October. Gasoline is comfortable; middle distillates are not, precisely where Russian outages and the capacity shortfall bite.
 
The surplus has yet to reach the tanks. Onshore inventories fell sharply (500mb) in 2026, remain below their five-year average, and have yet to be replenished. We therefore expect a smaller 2027 surplus than the IEA projects. Dated Brent should end 2027 near $78, within a $75-85 Brent range, with WTI in the mid-$70s to $80.
